questions.question: You are assigned to an antimicrobial stewardship program whose goals are to ensure the most efficient antibiotics are used and to prevent emergence of drug resistance.
questions.question_raw: 41. You are assigned to an antimicrobial stewardship program whose goals are to make sure the most efficient antibiotics are used and prevent emergence of drug resistance.

parts.text: List four essential components of such a program apart from education.

parts_raw.text: List 4 essential components of such a program apart from ''education''.

questions.model_answer: a) Per the CDC Core Elements (Mandell Table 51.2): (1) Leadership commitment – formal administrative support and dedicated staff time/resources; (2) Accountability – a single accountable program leader (e.g., an infectious diseases physician); (3) Drug expertise – a co-leading pharmacy leader; (4) Active stewardship actions/strategies – implementing at least one intervention (e.g., prospective audit and feedback, preauthorization, antibiotic time-out). Tracking and reporting of antibiotic use and resistance are the other two core elements.

cohort_answer.text: CDC: Leadership (dedicating necessary human, financial & IT resources); Accountability (appointing a leader responsible for program outcomes); Drug expertise (appointing a pharmacist leader responsible to improve abx use); Action (implementing at least one recommended action e.g. abx time-out); Tracking (monitoring abx prescription and resistance patterns); Reporting (regular reporting of tracking data to HCW); Education (educating physicians about optimal prescribing & resistance).

questions.question: Antibiotic consumption in healthcare facilities can be compared using defined daily doses (DDD) or days of therapy (DOT), the preferred surrogate.
questions.question_raw: 43. The consumption of antibiotics in healthcare establishments can be compared using defined daily doses (DDD) or days of therapy (DOT)= as per guidelines this is the preferred surrogate

parts.text: Give two reasons why DDD and DOT do not correlate perfectly every time.
For each, give one advantage it has over the other.

parts_raw.text: Give 2 reasons why they do not correlate perfectly every time.
b) For each, give one (1) advantage it has over the other.

questions.model_answer: a) Two reasons they do not correlate: (1) They measure different units – DDD uses grams dispensed divided by the fixed WHO defined daily dose, whereas DOT counts calendar days a patient receives at least one dose; (2) The WHO-assigned DDD often does not reflect the doses actually used in a given population (e.g., renal impairment, pediatrics, or locally higher/lower dosing), so grams-based DDD misestimates exposure while day-based DOT does not. b) DDD advantage: can be calculated from aggregate purchasing/pharmacy dispensing data without patient-level records, allowing easy benchmarking across institutions. DOT advantage: patient-level, not distorted by dose changes or renal/weight-based dosing, so it is more accurate and valid in children and renal patients (the preferred NHSN metric, reported as DOT per 1000 patient-days).
questions.beyond_mandell: The detailed DDD-vs-DOT comparison is from NHSN AUR module / Moehring et al. stewardship-metrics consensus; the chapter only names DOT per 1000 patient-days.

cohort_answer.text: Reasons for non-correlation: Different measures of abx used (DDD-grams, DOT-days); DDD is not patient level data, DOT requires patient level data; DDD will be inaccurate in renal insufficiency patients. Advantages: DDD - ability to compare across centers, can be calculated without computerized pharmacy records using purchasing data (cannot apply to children, weight-based dosing). DOT - can use in children, not affected by change in dosing or WHO DDD (preferred method).

questions.model_answer: a) (1) An infectious diseases physician (the accountable program leader); (2) A clinical pharmacist with antimicrobial/infectious diseases expertise (co-leader providing drug expertise). b) (1) Clinical microbiologist; (2) Infection control/hospital epidemiology practitioner; (3) Information systems/IT personnel (nursing is another acceptable member). c) (1) Preauthorization/preprescription approval of restricted agents; (2) Prospective audit and feedback (postprescription review with feedback); (3) Antibiotic time-outs; (4) IV-to-oral conversion programs; (5) Dose optimization; (6) Automatic stop orders (infection/syndrome-specific pathways and facility-specific guidelines are also acceptable).

cohort_answer.text: Central people: Clinical pharmacist; Infectious diseases physician. Other team members: Microbiologist, epidemiologist, research nurse, infection control physician/nurse. Strategies: Preauthorization/prospective audit and feedback; ASP intervention designed to reduce use of antibiotics associated with high risk CDI; Use PK monitoring and adjustment programs for aminoglycosides; Implement programs to increase use of oral antibiotics for initial therapy and timely transition from IV to PO; Implement guidelines and strategies to reduce antibiotic therapy to shortest effective duration; Develop facility specific clinical guidelines

questions.question: You are asked to assess vancomycin utilization at two hospitals. Hospital A: 2000 admissions, 4000 patient-days, 2000 g vancomycin used, 1000 days of vancomycin used. Hospital B: 1000 admissions, 2000 patient-days, 1000 g vancomycin used, 2000 days of vancomycin used. The WHO DDD for vancomycin is 2 g/day.
questions.question_raw: You are asked to assess the utilization of vancomycin at two hospitals. The following is given (table): Hospital A - Number of admissions: 2000, Number of patient-days: 4000, Grams of vancomycin used: 2000, Days of vancomycin used: 1000. Hospital B - Number of admissions: 1000, Number of patient-days: 2000, Grams of vancomycin used: 1000, Days of vancomycin used: 2000. The DDD for vancomycin as per WHO is 2g/day.

parts.text: Calculate the DDD per 1000 patient-days at hospital A.
Calculate the DOT for hospital B.
Name two situations where DOT is preferred.
The hospital administration asks which hospital is using vancomycin more appropriately. What is your response?

parts_raw.text: Calculate the DDD per 1000 patient-days at hospital A.
Calculate the DOT for hospital B.
Name two situations where DOT is preferred.
The hospital administration asks you which hospital is using vancomycin more appropriately. What is your response?

questions.model_answer: a) DDD = grams used ÷ WHO DDD = 2000 g ÷ 2 g/day = 1000 DDDs. Per 1000 patient-days = (1000 ÷ 4000) × 1000 = 250 DDD per 1000 patient-days. b) DOT for Hospital B = days of vancomycin ÷ patient-days × 1000 = (2000 ÷ 2000) × 1000 = 1000 DOT per 1000 patient-days (raw DOT = 2000 therapy-days). c) (1) Pediatric/weight-based dosing populations; (2) Renal impairment (or any setting with non-standard dosing), because the fixed WHO DDD misrepresents exposure whereas DOT does not. d) Neither metric measures appropriateness. By DDD, Hospital A uses less vancomycin (250 vs a higher normalized value at B), but utilization volume does not equal appropriateness; differences in case-mix, MRSA/dialysis/ICU populations, and dosing affect both use and the accuracy of the metrics. Patient-level review of indication, dosing, and de-escalation is required before judging which hospital prescribes more appropriately.
questions.beyond_mandell: DOT-preferred settings (pediatrics, renal impairment) reflect NHSN/WHO methodology; the chapter states only that NHSN reports DOT per 1000 patient-days.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort computed Hospital B DOT as 2000/4000×1000 = 500 using Hospital A's patient-days; with Hospital B's 2000 patient-days the correct normalized value is 1000 per 1000 patient-days.

cohort_answer.text: Hospital A DDD/1000PD: 2000g/2g=1000 DDD/4000 patient-days x1000 = 250 DDD per 1000 patient-days. Hospital B DOT: Days of use/patient days x1000 = 2000/4000 x1000 = 500 per 1000 patient-days. DOT preferred: pediatrics and renal impairment patients (WHO defined daily dose inaccurate in these populations). Response: Strictly by DDD criteria hospital A is using less vancomycin than hospital B (Hospital A DDD 250, Hospital B DDD 500); cannot directly correlate usage with appropriateness - other factors (patient population, MRSA rates, dialysis patients, pediatric units) may affect use or measurement accuracy; need patient-level data to make an informed comment.

questions.question: Defined daily doses (DDD) versus days of therapy (DOT).
questions.question_raw: 16. DDDs vs DOTs

parts.text: Give two reasons why DDD and DOT may not correlate with one another.
Name one advantage that DDD has over DOT.
Name one advantage that DOT has over DDD.

parts_raw.text: Two reasons why DDD and DOT may not correlate with one another?
Name one advantage that DDD has over DOT?
Name one advantage that DOT has over DDD?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Different units: DDD = grams dispensed ÷ the fixed WHO defined daily dose, whereas DOT counts days a patient received ≥1 dose, so single/intermittent doses (e.g., surgical prophylaxis) and dose intensity affect them differently; (2) The WHO DDD may not match doses actually given in the local population (renal impairment, pediatrics, higher local dosing), distorting DDD but not DOT. b) DDD is easier to obtain – it can be calculated from purchasing/dispensing data alone without patient-level administration records. c) DOT is more clinically accurate and is not affected by dose changes or WHO DDD assumptions, making it valid across populations including children and renal patients.
questions.beyond_mandell: Comparative detail is from NHSN AUR methodology; the chapter only references DOT per 1000 patient-days.

cohort_answer.text: Reasons: DDD (grams used/WHO approved values, may not reflect recommended doses) vs DOT (days receiving at least one dose, summed, may overestimate one-time doses e.g. surgical prophylaxis); DDD doses defined by WHO may not reflect actual patient population (peds/renal). DDD advantage: easier to obtain, relies on purchasing data without fine-tuned pharmacy administration data. DOT advantage: more accurate/clinically relevant, better for comparing multiple patient populations (though harder to obtain, favors broad spectrum monotherapy)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Clinical improvement / hemodynamic stability with defervescence (trending toward resolution, typically afebrile ~24 h); (2) A functioning GI tract able to absorb oral medication (tolerating oral intake, no vomiting/ileus/malabsorption); (3) An available oral agent with equivalent spectrum/susceptibility against the target organism (and no deep-seated infection requiring IV therapy).

questions.question: Two hospitals are compared using antibiotic consumption data including patient-days and days of therapy; calculate defined daily doses (DDD) and days of therapy (DOT) and interpret.
questions.question_raw: DDD and DOT question -> given two hospitals with numbers of patient days, days of therapy etc. and asked to calculate DDD and DOT

parts.text: Which population is DOT more reliable in?
Can you determine which hospital is using antibiotics more appropriately based on the antibiotic data alone?

parts_raw.text: Which population is DOT more reliable in?
Asked if you could determine which hospital is using abx more appropriately based on just the antibiotic data given.

questions.model_answer:
a) DOT counts each calendar day a patient actually receives an agent, independent of the dose given, so it is more reliable in populations where dosing deviates from the adult standard used to set the DDD — i.e. pediatric/weight-based dosing and patients with renal (or hepatic) impairment receiving reduced or atypical doses. (DDD, being grams used ÷ the assumed adult daily dose, systematically misestimates use in these groups.)
b) No. Aggregate consumption metrics (DDD or DOT per 1000 patient-days) quantify the volume of use and allow benchmarking, but do not capture appropriateness — they carry no information on clinical indication, infection prevalence, or case-mix of the populations served, so a lower number cannot be equated with better prescribing.
questions.beyond_mandell: The DDD/DOT definitions and the pediatric/renal caveat are standard WHO ATC/DDD and NHSN AUR-module metric conventions; Mandell p. 666 notes only measurement of use as DOT per 1000 patient-days and benchmarking via the NHSN AUR module.

questions.question: Antibiotic stewardship program strategies.
questions.question_raw: ASP question.

parts.text: Name the two strongest ASP strategies endorsed by the IDSA.
Name five others that can complement them.

parts_raw.text: Name the 2 strongest ASP strategies endorsed by the IDSA
Name 5 others that can complement

questions.model_answer:
a) The two core, evidence-based strategies are: (1) preauthorization / preprescription approval (prior-approval of restricted agents), and (2) prospective audit and feedback, also called postprescription review with feedback (PPRF).
b) Complementary strategies: (1) education of prescribers plus locally developed guidelines and clinical pathways; (2) antimicrobial formulary restriction; (3) pharmacy-driven interventions — intravenous-to-oral conversion and dose optimization; (4) streamlining / de-escalation and optimizing duration of therapy; (5) computer-assisted decision support / order entry (and automatic stop orders, antibiotic time-outs, syndrome-specific interventions).
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell identifies preauthorization and PPRF as the two core strategies and lists the complementary approaches (education, formulary restriction, IV-to-PO, streamlining, computer support); the “two core strategies” framing is from the IDSA/SHEA 2016 (Barlam) guideline, ref 16.

questions.question: Functions of an antimicrobial stewardship program.

parts.text: Name four functions of a stewardship program.

parts_raw.text: Name four functions of a stewardship program.

questions.model_answer: (1) Optimize clinical outcomes / improve appropriate antimicrobial use and patient care. (2) Minimize unintended consequences of antibiotic use — toxicity, adverse drug events and selection of pathogens such as Clostridioides difficile. (3) Reduce or stabilize antimicrobial resistance. (4) Reduce health-care costs without compromising quality of care.
questions.beyond_mandell: These are the IDSA/SHEA primary goals of stewardship; Mandell frames programs as improving patient care, reducing C. difficile and resistance, and containing cost (pp. 664-665).

cohort_answer.text: Optimize patient clinical outcomes. Minimize antibiotic adverse effects / toxicity. Reduce the selection of certain pathogenic organisms (e.g. Clostridium difficile). Reduce or stabilize antimicrobial resistance

questions.question_raw: Antimicrobial Stewardship

parts_raw.text: Name two core members of an antimicrobial stewardship team (per IDSA).
List 6 strategies to effectively conduct antimicrobial stewardship.
What are 3 persuasive interventions that can be utilized to limit antibiotic use?
What are 3 restrictive interventions that can be utilized to limit antibiotic use?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) An infectious diseases physician serving as the single accountable program leader; (2) a clinical pharmacist with infectious diseases expertise co-leading the program.
b) (1) Prospective audit and feedback (PPRF); (2) formulary restriction with preauthorization; (3) education plus locally developed guidelines/clinical pathways; (4) intravenous-to-oral conversion; (5) de-escalation/streamlining and dose optimization; (6) computer-assisted decision support/order entry with automatic stop orders.
c) Persuasive interventions: (1) dissemination of educational materials; (2) reminders at the point of prescribing; (3) audit and feedback (educational outreach/academic detailing).
d) Restrictive interventions: (1) preauthorization / prior approval of restricted agents; (2) formulary restriction of selected agents over a defined period; (3) time-sensitive automatic stop orders.
questions.beyond_mandell: Core team members (ID physician + ID pharmacist) are the IDSA/SHEA 2016 recommendation (ref 16), consistent with the CDC Core Elements “accountable leader” and “pharmacy leader” in Table 51.2 (p. 665); the persuasive/restrictive taxonomy is the Cochrane/EPOC classification (Davey, refs 71-72).

cohort_answer.text: Core members: Clinical ID physician, Clinical Pharmacist with ID training (also Clinical Microbiologist, IT specialist, Infection Control Professional, Hospital Epidemiologist). Strategies: 2 core (prospective audit with intervention/feedback, formulary restriction/preauthorization); supplemental (education, guidelines/clinical pathways, antimicrobial cycling, order forms, streamlining/de-escalation, dose optimization, IV to PO conversion). Persuasive interventions: dissemination of educational resources, reminders, audit and feedback, educational outreach. Restrictive: prior authorization, restriction of use in a period, time-sensitive automatic stop orders

questions.question: Days of therapy (DOT) and defined daily doses (DDD) are calculated for hospitals in your area. The DDD for vancomycin is 2 grams per day. Hospital A: 1000 patients, 4000 inpatient-days, 2000 g vancomycin, 1000 days on vancomycin. Hospital B: 2000 patients, 4000 inpatient-days, 4000 g vancomycin, 2000 days on vancomycin.
questions.question_raw: PM 12. Days of therapy (DOT) and Defined daily doses (DDD) are calculated for hospitals in your area. The DDD for vancomycin is 2 grams per day. Table: | Patient | Inpatient Days | Vanco (g) | Days on Vanco: Hospital A | 1000 | 4000 | 2000 | 1000; Hospital B | 2000 | 4000 | 4000 | 2000

parts.text: In Hospital A, what is the amount of DDD per 1000 patient-days?
In Hospital B, what is the DOT per 1000 patient-days?
What are two situations where DDD does not reflect DOT?
If a hospital administrator asks which hospital is using vancomycin better, what would you say?

parts_raw.text: In Hospital A what is the amount of DDD per 1000 patient days. (1)
In Hospital B what is the DOT per 1000 patient days (1)
What are two situations where DDD does not reflect DOT (1)
If a hospital administrator asks you which hospital is using vancomycin better what would you say (1)

questions.model_answer:
a) DDD = grams used ÷ DDD (2 g) = 2000 ÷ 2 = 1000 DDDs. Per 1000 patient-days = 1000 ÷ 4000 × 1000 = 250 DDD/1000 patient-days.
b) DOT/1000 patient-days = days on vancomycin ÷ inpatient-days × 1000 = 2000 ÷ 4000 × 1000 = 500 DOT/1000 patient-days.
c) (1) Pediatric / weight-based dosing and (2) renal (or hepatic) impairment or other atypical dosing — in both, the actual daily dose differs from the fixed adult DDD, so DDD over- or under-counts relative to the days actually treated (DOT).
d) Neither can be declared “better” from consumption data alone. These metrics measure volume of use, not appropriateness: they do not account for clinical indication, infection prevalence, or case-mix, so a lower DDD/DOT cannot be equated with better prescribing.
questions.beyond_mandell: DDD/DOT arithmetic follows WHO ATC/DDD and NHSN AUR conventions; Mandell p. 666 references DOT per 1000 patient-days and benchmarking but not the calculations.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort states Hospital B DOT = 1000/1000 patient-days, but with 2000 days on vancomycin over 4000 inpatient-days the correct value is 2000/4000 × 1000 = 500 DOT/1000 patient-days.

cohort_answer.text: Hospital A DDD/1000PD: 2000g/2g=1000 DDDs/4000 inpatient days=0.25x1000=250 (alt calc given for Hospital B: 4000g/2g=2000DDD/4000days=0.5x1000PD=500). Hospital B DOT/1000PD: 2000d/4000pt-days x1000=1000 DOT/1000PD (Hospital A calc: 1000/4000x1000=250 DOT/1000PD=0.25). DDD does not reflect DOT: pediatric/weight-based dosing, atypical dosing such as for renal dysfunction. Better hospital: Hospital A looks better on both DDD & DOT but no accounting for clinical indications or prevalence of infection types in populations served.

questions.model_answer:
a) Two core IDSA-recommended strategies: (1) preauthorization / preprescription approval, and (2) prospective audit and feedback (PPRF). Five complementary initiatives: (1) education plus local guidelines/clinical pathways; (2) formulary restriction; (3) intravenous-to-oral conversion; (4) de-escalation/streamlining and dose optimization; (5) computer-assisted decision support (with automatic stop orders / antibiotic time-outs).
b) DDD = total grams of an agent used ÷ the assumed standard adult daily dose, usually expressed per 1000 patient-days; it is easy to compute from pharmacy purchasing data but misestimates use with pediatric, weight-based or renal dosing. DOT = the number of calendar days a patient receives an agent (dose-independent), expressed per 1000 patient-days; it avoids the dosing-assumption error and is preferred in pediatric and renal-impairment populations, but requires patient-level data. Both measure volume of use, not appropriateness.
questions.beyond_mandell: The “two core strategies” framing is IDSA/SHEA 2016 (ref 16); DDD/DOT definitions follow WHO ATC/DDD and NHSN AUR conventions (Mandell references DOT/1000 patient-days on p. 666).

questions.question: Explain the post-antibiotic effect (PAE).

parts.text: Explain the post-antibiotic effect (PAE).

parts_raw.text: Explain PAE (postantibiotic effect).

questions.model_answer: The post-antibiotic effect is the persistent suppression of bacterial growth that continues after a brief (1-2 h) exposure to an antimicrobial, even once drug concentrations fall below the MIC — i.e., a delay before organisms recover and re-enter logarithmic growth. It is prominent with inhibitors of protein synthesis (aminoglycosides, macrolides, clindamycin, tetracyclines) and nucleic-acid synthesis (fluoroquinolones, rifampin); beta-lactams show a significant PAE mainly against gram-positive cocci. Proposed mechanisms include non-lethal cellular damage requiring repair and persistence of drug at its target. A prolonged PAE permits extended dosing intervals (e.g., once-daily aminoglycosides).
questions.beyond_mandell: PAE concept is standard PK/PD (Mandell antimicrobial pharmacodynamics chapter); not covered in the stewardship text read.

cohort_answer.text: Post-antibiotic effect - persistent suppression of bacterial growth after brief exposure of 1-2 hours to antibiotic. Delay before microorganisms recover and re-enter log-growth period post exposure. Generally seen with inhibitors of protein synthesis (AGs, macrolides/clindamycin, tetracyclines, rifampin) and nucleic acid synthesis (FQs). Beta lactams produce minor effect only for GP. Mechanisms may include nonlethal damage, persistence of ABx at site of action.

questions.question: Defined daily dose (DDD) and days of therapy (DOT) as metrics in antimicrobial stewardship.
questions.question_raw: ASP: DDD (defined daily dose) and DOT (days of therapy) in antimicrobial stewardship

parts.text: Give 2 reasons why the DDD and DOT values might not be the same.
Give 1 advantage of each.

parts_raw.text: A. Give 2 reasons why they might not be the same
B. Give 1 advantage of each

questions.model_answer: a) (1) DDD depends on the dose prescribed (an actual dose higher or lower than the WHO assumed daily dose inflates or deflates the DDD count), whereas DOT counts any dose in a 24-h period as one day regardless of amount. (2) DDD misclassifies populations dosed differently from the adult standard (renal adjustment, pediatrics), so the same days of therapy yield a different DDD total. b) DDD advantage: can be derived from aggregate pharmacy purchasing/dispensing data without electronic patient-level records, enabling benchmarking between institutions. DOT advantage: unaffected by dose or dose adjustments, allowing accurate comparison across different patient populations (e.g., renal, pediatric).
questions.beyond_mandell: DDD/DOT definitions and their relative merits are from WHO ATC/DDD and NHSN methodology, not the stewardship text read.

cohort_answer.text:
DDD: assumed average maintenance dose per day for main indication in adults (WHO). Example: Levofloxacin 500mg po od x7 days = 7 DDD; 750mg po od x7 days = 10.5 DDD. DOT: number of days patient receives antimicrobial regardless of dose; any dose in 24h = 1 DOT. Example: Levofloxacin 500mg or 750mg od x7 days = 7 DOT each; combined with Vancomycin 1g iv q12h x7 days = 14 total DOT. They differ because DDD varies with dose while DOT does not.
DDD advantage: Provides method to benchmark within/between institutions if normalized to patient days; can be calculated without computerized pharmacy records using purchasing data. DOT advantage: Not affected by change in dosing; allows multiple patient populations to be compared accurately.

questions.model_answer:
a) Aminoglycosides show concentration-dependent killing and a postantibiotic effect; high-dose once-daily dosing maximizes the peak/MIC and 24-hour AUC/MIC ratios (efficacy rises as peak/MIC exceeds 8-10) while the drug-free interval limits saturable proximal-tubular uptake, giving equal or better efficacy with less nephrotoxicity.
b) Beta-lactams show time-dependent killing, so efficacy depends on the time free concentration remains above the MIC (T>MIC); continuous infusion maximizes T>MIC for an organism with a borderline/intermediate MIC, whereas intermittent q6h dosing has troughs that fall below the MIC.
c) Vancomycin efficacy tracks the AUC/MIC ratio; more frequent (q8h) dosing achieves the target AUC with lower peaks, theoretically reducing toxicity while maintaining exposure.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the once-daily aminoglycoside principle is grounded in this chapter; the piperacillin-tazobactam (beta-lactam T>MIC) and vancomycin (AUC/MIC) pharmacodynamics come from general antimicrobial PK/PD, not the aminoglycoside chapter.

cohort_answer.text: a) Higher dose extended interval dosing of gentamicin achieves higher peak levels while avoiding toxic trough levels; potentially lower risk of nephrotoxicity based on animal studies (no difference in ototoxicity); post-antibiotic effect with ongoing killing after concentration drops below MIC; convenience of once daily dosing/monitoring; equivalent clinical efficacy. b) Continuous infusion: reduced mortality in meta-analysis (greater efficacy), also observed with prolonged infusion duration vs traditional dosing; can use lower total daily dose to maintain T>MIC. c) Shorter dosing interval (TID/q8h) allows target AUC/MIC to be achieved with lower loading doses, keeping peaks lower; theoretically reduces nephrotoxicity.

questions.question: A Monte Carlo simulation models an antimicrobial against Staphylococcus aureus at different MICs. The table shows that at an MIC of 0.25 mg/L, 94.2% of isolates are inhibited, and at an MIC of 0.12 mg/L, 99.9% of isolates are inhibited.

parts.text: Define AUC/MIC.

parts_raw.text: Define AUC/MIC
What is one class of antimicrobials whose clinical efficacy is predicted by AUC/MIC?
Based on table, what is the appropriate MIC Breakpoint and why?

questions.model_answer:
a) AUC/MIC is the ratio of the area under the free (unbound) drug concentration-time curve over 24 hours (fAUC0-24) to the MIC of the organism; it is the PK/PD index that predicts efficacy for agents whose killing depends on total drug exposure rather than peak or time above MIC.
b) Fluoroquinolones (AUC/MIC is the driver of efficacy; vancomycin/glycopeptides are also AUC/MIC-predicted).
c) An MIC breakpoint of 0.25 mg/L is appropriate: it captures the wild-type susceptible population (94.2% of isolates inhibited) at a value where the achievable AUC/MIC target is reliably met, while lowering the breakpoint to 0.12 adds only marginal coverage (99.9%) and would misclassify many wild-type isolates as resistant. The breakpoint should separate the susceptible wild-type distribution from resistant organisms while corresponding to an MIC at which the standard regimen achieves the PK/PD target (high probability of target attainment).
questions.beyond_mandell: PK/PD indices and MIC breakpoint/PTA concepts from Craig WA and CLSI/EUCAST breakpoint methodology; not covered in this stewardship chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text: AUC/MIC is the steady state drug area under the curve ratio to MIC which predicts efficacy of antimicrobial based on total concentration of drug achieved over 24h. Class: Glycopeptides. MIC breakpoint: table shows PTA (probability of target attainment) % at each MIC; to define AUC/MIC from table you need the actual drug regimen (e.g. ceftobiprole example: 250mg q12h achieved T>MIC 30% 100% of the time when MIC<2; if MIC 4, 250mg BID was not enough, would require 750mg BID to achieve 30% PTA for MIC 4, assuming T>MIC 30% required for 100% killing).

parts.text: Identify which curve represents AUC/MIC < 100.

Name 2 antibiotics that follow these principles (time dependent and concentration dependent). Justify your response pharmacologically.

questions.model_answer:
a) AUC/MIC < 100 represents inadequate drug exposure, so it is the curve with the worst outcome — the line showing the least bacterial killing and poorest survival (lowest on the survival/highest on the residual-bacteria axis).
b) (1) Concentration-dependent: aminoglycosides (or fluoroquinolones) - rate and extent of killing increase with higher peak/AUC relative to MIC (Cmax/MIC and AUC/MIC are the drivers), and a prolonged post-antibiotic effect permits extended (once-daily) dosing intervals. (2) Time-dependent: beta-lactams (or linezolid) - killing depends on maintaining free drug concentration above the MIC for a sufficient fraction of the dosing interval (fT>MIC), with no added benefit from higher peaks once saturating concentrations are reached; efficacy is maximized by prolonging exposure (e.g., extended or continuous infusion).
questions.beyond_mandell: Concentration- vs time-dependent killing, post-antibiotic effect, and fT>MIC/AUC-MIC targets from Craig WA PK/PD framework; not in this stewardship chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text: AUC/MIC <100 would have poorest survival - the line furthest down on the KM graph (specific graph not included with source). Time-dependent: Beta-lactams, erythromycin. Concentration-dependent: aminoglycosides, quinolones. Concentration-dependent killing (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, daptomycin) - rate/extent of killing increases with peak concentration, also exhibit post-antibiotic effect allowing longer dosing intervals. Time-dependent killing (all beta-lactams, linezolid) - free concentration maintained above MIC for a drug-specific fraction of time between doses achieves efficacy; maximizing duration of exposure (e.g. continuous infusion) leads to greater efficacy.

questions.question: Explain how understanding of antimicrobial pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic principles can be applied to optimize therapy in a critically ill ICU patient.

parts.text: Give three good reasons how this knowledge will help treat your patient in the ICU.

Three graphs plot log kill (y-axis) against time (x-axis): two depict AUC/MIC-driven killing and one depicts time-dependent killing. Identify which shows the greatest log kill, justify your response, and give an example of an antibiotic that follows this principle.

parts_raw.text: Give 3 good reasons how this knowledge will help treat your patient in the ICU

3 graphs – y axis log kill, x axis time, 2 of the graphs AUC/MIC, one of them time/AUC. Which shows the greatest log kill, justify your response. Give an example of an antibiotic that follows this principle.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Use high-dose, extended-interval (once-daily) aminoglycoside dosing to maximize the Cmax/MIC ratio and killing while reducing nephro/ototoxicity, exploiting the post-antibiotic effect. (2) Use extended or continuous infusion of beta-lactams to maximize fT>MIC, which is especially important in the ICU where augmented renal clearance and increased volume of distribution lower drug levels. (3) Target an adequate AUC/MIC for vancomycin (e.g., AUC-guided dosing) to optimize efficacy against S. aureus while minimizing nephrotoxicity, and use therapeutic drug monitoring to individualize exposure in altered ICU pharmacokinetics.
b) The concentration-dependent (AUC/MIC) graph shows the greatest log kill, because the rate and extent of killing rise as concentration/exposure increase above the MIC; the time-dependent agent plateaus once concentration exceeds the MIC and shows no further increase in killing at higher concentrations. Example of a concentration-dependent (AUC/MIC) agent: an aminoglycoside (or a fluoroquinolone); the time-dependent example is a beta-lactam.
questions.beyond_mandell: ICU PK/PD dose optimization (extended-interval aminoglycosides, prolonged-infusion beta-lactams, AUC-guided vancomycin) from Craig WA and vancomycin consensus (ASHP/IDSA/SIDP 2020); not in this stewardship chapter slice.

cohort_answer.text: Higher dose, extended interval dosing of aminoglycosides to optimize efficacy and reduce adverse effects; Continuous/extended infusion of beta-lactams to reduce total daily dose and minimize toxicities; Optimize AUC/MIC for Vancomycin (if measuring AUC) to improve efficacy without risking toxicity; take advantage of Post-Antibiotic Effect with aminoglycosides (lower frequency dosing, effect continues even after drug is gone). || AUC/MIC - Vancomycin; Time/AUC - all beta-lactams. Graphs demonstrate concentration-dependent killing with more rapid killing at higher concentrations; beta-lactams do not show significant change in killing once sufficient MIC is achieved to prevent growth.

questions.question: Regarding antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs):
questions.question_raw: In terms of ASP

parts.text: What are two recommended core ASP interventions (as described in IDSA guidelines and Mandell)?
What are five other interventions?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 recommended ASP interventions (these are in the IDSA and Mandell)
What are 5 other interventions.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Preauthorization / preprescription approval (PPA) - physicians must obtain approval before a restricted antimicrobial is released. (2) Prospective audit and feedback, also called postprescription review with feedback (PPRF) - review of targeted antimicrobial prescriptions 2-3 days/week coupled with educational, evidence-based feedback to the prescriber.
b) (1) Intravenous-to-oral switch. (2) Dose optimization based on PK/PD principles (e.g., aminoglycoside monitoring). (3) Automatic stop orders / optimizing duration of therapy. (4) Formulary restriction (limiting agents available on formulary). (5) Education plus locally developed guidelines and clinical pathways. (Other acceptable: antibiotic time-outs, requiring documentation of an indication, infection/syndrome-specific pathways, and computer-assisted decision support.)

cohort_answer.text: IV/PO switch; minimize duration; minimize C.diffogenic antibiotics; prospective audit and feedback; dissemination; educational resource; reminders; antibiograms; PK monitoring of aminoglycosides.
